newsitem.title: ITALY: Deal seen on Italy, Spain EMU delay - Italian paper.
newsitem.headline: Deal seen on Italy, Spain EMU delay - Italian paper.

text.p: A deal is taking shape between Germany and France on keeping Italy and Spain out of the first wave of members of a planned European economic and monetary union (EMU), an Italian financial daily reported on Wednesday.

France had come round to the idea of keeping Italy and Spain out of the group of EMU front-runners because it feared that Germany would otherwise insist on a two-year delay in launching the currency, said the report from Milan daily Il Sole 24 Ore's Frankfurt correspondent, quoting "sources in Bonn".

"Thanks to the threat, still latent, of a two-year delay in the Euro, Bonn has managed in the last weeks to convince Paris of the importance that Germany attaches to the temporary exclusion of Italy from the first group of single currency countries," the report said.
"But since it is considered politically too risky to abandon Italy as the only excluded one together with Greece, (the idea of) similar treatment for Spain is gaining ground," the report added.
French President Jacques Chirac was seeking assurances that any delay imposed on Italy and Spain should not have negative financial consequences for France.

"He has therefore renewed the request for a Frenchman at the head of the European central bank, in the person, it appears, of the Director General of the International Monetary Fund, Michel Camdessus," the report added.
Italy is struggling to wrestle its public sector borrowing requirement down to three percent of gross domestic product by the end of the year in an effort to meet a key qualifyuing criterion for EMU.
But there have been doubts as to the sustainability of the deficit-cutting measures imposed by Italy in recent months.

The European Monetary Institute (EMI) in an annual report released on Tuesday lashed out at one-off measures to reduce deficit to GDP ratios, saying they "cannot be regarded as contributing to sustainability" but it did not specifically mention Italy.

Some Italian leaders, including Massimo D'Alema, secretary of the left-wing PDS party which is part of the centre-left government coalition, did not appear as strongly opposed to Italy staying out of the first wave of EMU members as Prime Minister Romano Prodi, who is determined to join at the start, Il Sole said.
